subject: english-literature
title: Sexuality, the Body and the Victorian Vampire
welcome_lead: Examine how Stoker codes female desire, queer transgression, and bodily penetration through the figure of the vampire.
meta_desc: A-Level Edexcel adventure on sexuality, gender, and the body in Stoker's Dracula: Lucy, Mina, and the vampire kiss.
final_note: The vampire bite is a Victorian thought-experiment about everything official discourse cannot say about sex.

concepts.def: Penetrative, mouth-to-throat, fluid-exchanging; Christopher Craft reads it as coded queer/heterosexual transgression.
Lucy moves from chaste fiancée to predatory 'bloofer lady'; her staking is staged with explicit sexual violence.
Mina, partially vamped, retains agency, drives the documentary archive, and locates Dracula via hypnotic link.
The female vampires at Castle Dracula who attempt to seduce Harker; embody overt female sexual aggression.
Craft's 'Kiss Me with Those Red Lips' (1984) reads the vampire's mouth as a site of unstable gender and queer desire.
Lucy receives blood from Arthur, Seward, Van Helsing, and Quincey — a quasi-sexual circulation Arthur calls a 'marriage'.

walkthroughs.body_html: Christopher Craft's 1984 essay 'Kiss Me with Those Red Lips' (in Representations) reads the vampire bite as a queered erotic act: mouths penetrate, bodies bleed, gender roles invert. Harker, on the threshold of Castle Dracula, fears and desires the three sisters in 'languorous ecstasy'. Stoker registers homoerotic and heteroerotic anxiety simultaneously, using the supernatural as alibi.

Lucy's staking by Arthur Holmwood at the Kingstead crypt is rendered with extraordinary sexual specificity: 'the body shook and quivered and twisted in wild contortions'. Critics including Phyllis Roth and Carol Senf read it as a ritual restoration of patriarchal order: the sexually awakened woman must be killed by her fiancé, with male witnesses, before she can be 'truly dead'. The Victorian double standard is dramatised as ritual.

Mina Murray Harker exemplifies Stoker's ambivalent New Woman. She masters shorthand, typing, and Bradshaw's railway guide; she organises the male hunters' archive. Yet she is also figured as 'mother' to the group, and her vampiric infection by Dracula at Carfax is rendered as sexual assault. Critics including Carol Senf argue Mina embodies Stoker's attempt to incorporate female competence while reaffirming domestic boundaries.
